course.title: Scaling a Startup
course.description: Turning a product that works into a company that grows - how founders scale a startup into an enduring business without breaking what made it work. This course covers the line between a startup and a scale-up, when it is safe to scale, how to grow the team, culture, systems, and go-to-market, and how to raise growth capital and lead through change. Structure and framing draw on the Startup company article from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: A startup is best described as an organization designed to...
options: run a proven business at steady state
search for a repeatable and scalable business model
maximize short-term profit from day one
questions.explanation: A startup is a young company set up to find a repeatable, scalable model under heavy uncertainty - its first job is learning, not steady operation.

questions.prompt: A company shifts from startup to scale-up mainly once it has...
options: a large office and a logo
found product-market fit and a repeatable model
questions.explanation: Product-market fit - durable, repeating demand - is the usual dividing line, not size or funding.

questions.prompt: Premature scaling, highlighted by the Startup Genome research, means...
options: scaling only after strong product-market fit
spending and growing ahead of a proven model
scaling the product but not the team
scaling too slowly for the market
questions.explanation: Premature scaling is pouring fuel on a model that has not been proven yet, and Startup Genome found it the most common cause of startup failure.

questions.prompt: As a team grows past roughly 10 to 15 people, founders usually must...
options: delegate and add structure and managers
do all the important work themselves
remove every process to stay nimble
questions.explanation: Direct coordination breaks down at that size, so founders delegate and introduce light org structure.

questions.prompt: Company culture during fast growth is best protected by...
options: writing values down and hiring, promoting, and firing for them
ignoring it until the company is big
questions.explanation: Culture spreads by osmosis in a tiny team; at scale it must be made explicit and reinforced by who you hire, promote, and let go.

questions.prompt: A sales engine that can scale is one that is...
options: built around a single star seller
repeatable, with a defined process a new rep can follow
driven only by word of mouth
questions.explanation: A scalable sales engine is a documented, repeatable motion, so adding reps predictably adds revenue.

questions.prompt: Growth-stage capital, such as a Series B or later round, is typically raised to...
options: pour fuel on a model that already works
cover a permanent lack of revenue
questions.explanation: Growth rounds accelerate a proven, repeatable model rather than fund the search for one.

questions.prompt: As a company scales, the founder's role usually shifts from...
options: doing the work to building the organization that does the work
strategy to no role at all
questions.explanation: The founder moves from doing the work personally to designing the team, systems, and leaders that do it.

lessons.title: Startup or scale-up? Knowing which company you are
lessons.grammar_note: Use 'startup' for the search phase and 'scale-up' for the growth phase; the hyphen in scale-up is standard, and the dividing line is product-market fit, not headcount.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell a startup apart from a scale-up, explain the dividing line between them, and place a real company on that path. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what single milestone most clearly marks the move from startup to scale-up, and why is it not the amount of money raised?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A startup is a young organization built to search for a repeatable and scalable business model under heavy uncertainty. Its real job is learning: who the customer is, what problem they will pay to solve, and how to reach them profitably. A scale-up is what a startup becomes once that search has largely succeeded. The usual dividing line is product-market fit - clear, repeating evidence that a defined market wants the product, buys it, and comes back for more. Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia describes a startup as a company in the early stages of operations, founded to develop a scalable business model. A scale-up keeps that ambition but changes the central question from 'does this work?' to 'how far and how fast can this grow?' One common marker, used by the OECD, defines a scale-up as a firm that grows revenue or headcount by more than 20 percent a year for three straight years. The change is not only about size. It is a shift in what the company optimizes for: a startup optimizes for learning and survival, while a scale-up optimizes for the efficient, repeatable growth of a model it already trusts.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Think of three stages. First, problem-solution fit: you confirm a real problem exists. Second, product-market fit: a specific segment buys repeatedly and would miss the product if it vanished. Third, scale: you grow the proven model. Example: a software company spends two years testing pricing, messaging, and features with early customers. Churn is high and every sale feels custom - still a startup. Then one segment, say mid-size clinics, starts renewing at over 90 percent and referring peers. The model now repeats, so hiring five more sales reps predictably produces more revenue. That company has crossed into scale-up territory. Another example: a food brand that sells well at one local market is validated but not yet scalable; only once it proves the same product sells through national retail with stable unit economics can it truly scale. Signals of a scale-up include a predictable customer acquisition cost, a payback period you can forecast, strong retention, and more demand than you can serve. Signals you are still a startup include constant pivots, custom-feeling deals, and no reliable way to repeat your wins.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each, then check yourself. 1) In one sentence, what is a startup searching for? 2) What milestone usually separates a startup from a scale-up? 3) Name one quantitative marker of a scale-up. 4) A company renews one segment at 92 percent and can forecast its acquisition cost - startup or scale-up? 5) Why is a single strong local market not proof of scalability? 6) What does a startup optimize for, versus a scale-up? Answers: 1) A repeatable and scalable business model. 2) Product-market fit. 3) Growth above 20 percent a year in revenue or headcount for three years (OECD). 4) A scale-up, because the model now repeats predictably. 5) Because scalability means the same model works across many markets with stable economics, not just one favorable spot. 6) A startup optimizes for learning and survival; a scale-up optimizes for efficient, repeatable growth.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating a fundraise as the line between startup and scale-up - money is fuel, not proof, and plenty of well-funded companies never find fit. Mistake: assuming more size means scale-up; a large firm whose every deal is custom and unrepeatable is still searching. Mistake: declaring early traction to be product-market fit too soon, which sets up premature scaling later. Mistake: thinking the shift happens on a single day rather than as a gradual, evidence-backed transition. Exit: (a) What is the real dividing line between a startup and a scale-up? (b) True or false: raising a big round makes you a scale-up. Answers: product-market fit, shown by repeatable and durable demand; false - funding is fuel, not evidence that the model works.

lessons.title: When to scale: fit first, and the trap of premature scaling
lessons.grammar_note: Treat scaling as a gas pedal, not a steering wheel: it multiplies whatever model you already have, so press it only after product-market fit, never to find it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Decide whether a company is ready to scale, and recognize premature scaling before it becomes fatal. Warm-up: if growing faster multiplies your current model, what happens when you multiply a model that loses money on every customer?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Scaling means deliberately spending to grow faster - more hiring, more marketing, more inventory - in the belief that each dollar in will reliably return more than a dollar out. That bet only pays off after product-market fit. Scale before it and you simply multiply a broken model, burning cash faster the better your fundraising goes. The Startup Genome project, which studied thousands of internet companies, found that premature scaling is the single most common reason startups fail. Its research reported that most failed startups had scaled at least one dimension of the business - team, customers, product, or spend - far ahead of the others, growing headcount and marketing before the model could support them. The signal that it is time to scale is consistency: a repeatable sales process, retention that holds, an acquisition cost you can predict and recover, and more demand than you can meet. The signal to wait is noise: every deal is custom, customers leak out the back through churn, and growth depends on founder heroics. Readiness is earned with evidence, not with optimism or a full bank account.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Startup Genome describes scaling across several dimensions that must stay in balance: customer acquisition, team size, product scope, and spend. Premature scaling is when one of these races ahead of the rest. Example: a company raises a large round, hires 30 salespeople, and triples its marketing budget while monthly churn is still 8 percent. New customers pour in the front door and leak straight out the back; burn accelerates and runway disappears. Contrast that with a company that waits until churn falls to 2 percent and one rep reliably closes a forecastable number of deals, then adds reps one cohort at a time, checking that the economics still hold. A practical readiness checklist: (1) retention curves flatten rather than fall to zero; (2) acquisition cost is recovered within a sensible payback window; (3) referrals and repeat purchases appear on their own; (4) the sales motion is written down so a new hire can follow it. Ramp spending only while each check stays green as volume rises - and ease off the moment one turns red.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each, then check yourself. 1) According to Startup Genome, what is the most common reason startups fail? 2) Name two of the dimensions that must scale in balance. 3) Why does scaling a high-churn business make things worse? 4) Give one concrete signal that a company is ready to scale. 5) Is a full bank account enough reason to scale? 6) Should you add 30 reps at once or a cohort at a time, and why? Answers: 1) Premature scaling. 2) Any two of: customer acquisition, team size, product scope, spend. 3) Because you pay to acquire customers who leave before they pay back their cost, so faster growth burns cash faster. 4) Flattening retention, recoverable acquisition cost, organic referrals, or a documented sales motion. 5) No - money is fuel, not evidence of fit. 6) A cohort at a time, so you can confirm the economics hold before committing more.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: scaling to find product-market fit instead of after it, which is the textbook definition of premature scaling. Mistake: scaling one dimension - usually headcount or marketing - far ahead of the others, breaking the balance Startup Genome warns about. Mistake: reading a single big month as proof of fit. Mistake: ignoring unit economics because top-line growth looks impressive. Exit: (a) What must come before scaling? (b) Name the failure pattern where spend and growth run ahead of a proven model. Answers: product-market fit, backed by repeatable evidence; premature scaling.

lessons.title: Scaling the team and protecting culture
lessons.grammar_note: Delegation means handing over the outcome and the authority, not just the task; if you keep the decision, you have assigned work, not delegated it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Plan hiring and delegation as a team grows, choose a basic org design, and protect culture through fast growth. Warm-up: if a founder makes every decision, what breaks first when the team doubles - speed, quality, or morale?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A small team coordinates by talking; everyone hears everything. As headcount climbs past roughly a dozen people, that stops working, and founders must do two hard things: delegate and add structure. Delegation means handing someone the outcome and the authority to pursue it, then holding them accountable to the result - not hovering over every task. Org design is how you group people so that work flows: usually functional teams (product, sales, operations, support) with managers who own outcomes and shield their teams from noise. Each new management layer trades some speed for more capacity and clearer ownership. Hiring shifts too: early hires are generalists who thrive in chaos, while scale-up hires are specialists who bring proven playbooks. Culture is the set of behaviors a company rewards and tolerates. In a tiny team it spreads by osmosis; at scale it must be made explicit through written values and, more importantly, through who you hire, promote, reward, and let go. People watch what you do far more than what you post on the wall. Structure and culture are the invisible machinery that lets a company grow without grinding to a halt.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Example of delegation done right: a founder stops approving every refund and instead gives support a clear policy plus authority to decide, keeping only the rare escalations. Decisions get faster and the founder reclaims hours. Example of org design: at 8 people everyone reports to the founder; at 40, five managers each own a function and the founder meets a leadership team instead of forty individuals. Hiring example: the first salesperson is a scrappy generalist who figures out the motion; the tenth is a specialist who scales a motion that already works - hiring them in the wrong order fails. Culture example: a company that claims to value quality but always promotes the fastest shippers will, in practice, teach everyone that speed beats quality. To protect culture, define three to five values as observable behaviors, bake them into interviews and performance reviews, and act on them even when it is expensive - letting go of a high performer who violates them says more than any handbook.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each, then check yourself. 1) What two things must a founder do as the team grows past a dozen? 2) What makes delegation different from simply assigning a task? 3) Why do early and late hires differ? 4) Name one way a company signals its real culture. 5) What does each new management layer trade away, and gain? 6) How should written values connect to hiring and promotion? Answers: 1) Delegate and add structure. 2) Delegation hands over the outcome and the authority, not just the to-do. 3) Early hires are generalists for chaos; later hires are specialists who scale proven playbooks. 4) Who it hires, promotes, rewards, and lets go. 5) It trades some speed for more capacity and clearer ownership. 6) Values should drive interview questions, promotion criteria, and performance reviews, not just hang on a wall.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: fake delegation, where you hand over the task but keep the decision, so nothing truly moves off your plate. Mistake: hiring senior specialists before the motion exists for them to scale, or keeping only generalists long after the company needs depth. Mistake: adding management layers so fast that the company turns slow and political. Mistake: writing values you contradict in your promotions, which quietly teaches the opposite. Exit: (a) What is the difference between delegating and assigning? (b) Where does culture actually live - on the wall or in decisions? Answers: delegation includes authority and ownership of the outcome, assigning does not; culture lives in the decisions you make about people, especially hiring, promoting, and firing.

lessons.title: Scaling systems, processes, and operations
lessons.grammar_note: Document first, then standardize, then automate: never automate a process you have not yet written down and simplified, or you just make the mess run faster.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Spot where informal coordination is breaking, turn recurring work into documented processes, and decide what to standardize or automate as volume grows. Warm-up: what tasks in a growing company only the founder knows how to do, and why is that a risk?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: In a small company, work gets done through memory and hallway conversations. As volume rises, that breaks: handoffs get dropped, quality drifts, and the founder becomes the single point of failure because the important knowledge lives only in their head. The fix is to turn recurring work into processes - written, repeatable ways of doing a job the same way every time - and then encode the most stable ones into systems and tools. The healthy order is document, standardize, automate. First write down how the work is actually done. Then simplify and standardize it so anyone can follow it. Only then automate the parts that are stable and high volume, so you speed up a clean process rather than a messy one. The aim is not bureaucracy; it is to free people from re-deciding routine things so they can spend judgment where it matters. Good operations make the business predictable: an order, a hire, or a support ticket flows through the same reliable path whether it is the tenth or the ten-thousandth. Process should scale capacity without adding friction, and it should be revisited as the company grows rather than frozen in place.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Example of a single point of failure: only the founder can configure a new customer account, so onboarding stalls every time they travel. Writing a step-by-step runbook lets anyone do it, and a template or tool later removes most of the steps entirely. Example of document-then-automate: a finance lead first writes the monthly invoicing checklist, finds three redundant steps, removes them, and only then automates the remaining flow - automating the original mess would have locked in the waste. A key idea is the difference between a process (the agreed steps) and a tool (the software that carries them out); buying software without agreeing the process just automates confusion. Watch for signs you need process: the same mistakes recur, new hires take months to become useful, or quality depends on who happens to do the work. A useful rule: if a task will be done more than a handful of times, write it down; if it is done constantly and never changes, consider automating it. Keep processes light enough that people follow them, and review them as scale changes what good looks like.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each, then check yourself. 1) What is the healthy order for handling recurring work? 2) Why is it risky when only the founder can do a task? 3) What is the difference between a process and a tool? 4) Why should you simplify a process before automating it? 5) Name two signs a team needs more process. 6) When is automation worth it? Answers: 1) Document, then standardize, then automate. 2) It makes the founder a single point of failure and stalls the business when they are unavailable. 3) A process is the agreed set of steps; a tool is the software that carries them out. 4) So you speed up a clean process instead of locking in waste. 5) Any two of: recurring mistakes, slow ramp for new hires, quality that depends on who does the work. 6) When the task is high volume, stable, and already documented and simplified.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: automating a broken process, which just makes the mess run faster and harder to fix. Mistake: buying tools before agreeing on the process, so the software encodes confusion. Mistake: adding so much process that people route around it, which is worse than having none. Mistake: writing processes once and freezing them, even as scale changes what good looks like. Exit: (a) In what order should you document, standardize, and automate? (b) Why is buying software not the same as fixing a process? Answers: document first, then standardize, then automate; because software only executes steps, so without an agreed, simplified process it just automates the existing confusion.

questions.explanation: Fit - repeatable, durable demand - marks the move from searching to scaling, not size or funding.

questions.prompt: Startup Genome identified which pattern as the most common cause of startup failure?
questions.explanation: Scaling ahead of a proven model - premature scaling - was the top failure pattern in their study.

questions.prompt: Scaling a business with high churn tends to...
options: burn cash faster as paid-for customers leave
questions.explanation: You keep paying to acquire customers who leave before they pay back, so faster growth burns cash faster.

lessons.title: Scaling go-to-market, the sales engine, and customer experience
lessons.grammar_note: A 'sales engine' is a process, not a person: if revenue depends on one star seller, you have a hero, not an engine, and heroes do not scale.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe a scalable go-to-market motion and sales engine, and explain how to keep quality and customer experience high as volume grows. Warm-up: if your best salesperson left tomorrow, how much of your revenue process would leave with them?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Go-to-market is how a company reaches, wins, and keeps customers: the channels it uses, the message it leads with, and the motion by which a stranger becomes a paying, renewing customer. Early on, founders sell by instinct and charm. To scale, that instinct must become a sales engine - a repeatable, documented process with defined stages, so that a newly hired rep can follow it and predictably produce results. When the engine works, adding reps or marketing spend produces forecastable growth; when it does not, hiring more sellers just multiplies confusion. But winning customers is only half the job. As volume rises, the experience that made early customers love you - fast answers, careful onboarding, personal attention - comes under strain. Maintaining quality and customer experience at scale means investing in support, onboarding, and clear service standards before cracks appear, so that the thousandth customer is treated as well as the tenth. Growth that wins customers at the front while eroding their experience at the back leaks them out through churn, which quietly destroys the very economics that justified scaling. A durable scale-up grows acquisition and experience together.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: A sales engine breaks selling into stages - for example lead, qualified, demo, proposal, closed - each with a definition of what moves a deal forward. Example: a company writes its playbook so that a new rep ramps in weeks instead of months and hits a forecastable quota; now hiring five reps reliably adds revenue. Contrast the hero problem: one gifted founder closes everything, so the company cannot grow sales without cloning them, which is impossible. On the experience side, example: a support team that answered every email in minutes at 50 customers must, at 5,000, add help docs, tiered support, and clear response-time standards so quality does not collapse. A useful pairing is customer acquisition cost against lifetime value: scaling is healthy only when the value a customer brings comfortably exceeds the cost to win them, and that stays true only if experience keeps them renewing. Build the engine and the experience in parallel: a faster front door with a leaking back door just drains the tank more quickly.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each, then check yourself. 1) What is a sales engine, in one sentence? 2) Why is a single star seller a scaling problem? 3) Name two stages a sales process might define. 4) What happens to economics when growth erodes customer experience? 5) How might a support team preserve quality as customers multiply? 6) Why compare acquisition cost against lifetime value? Answers: 1) A repeatable, documented selling process any trained rep can follow to produce predictable results. 2) Because revenue depends on one irreplaceable person, so the motion cannot be copied or scaled. 3) Any two of: lead, qualified, demo, proposal, closed. 4) Customers churn out the back, draining the economics that justified scaling. 5) With help docs, tiered support, and clear response-time standards. 6) To confirm each customer is worth more than it costs to win and keep them.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: hiring a pile of salespeople before a repeatable motion exists, so you scale confusion instead of revenue. Mistake: treating marketing spend as a growth lever while the engine is still broken. Mistake: letting onboarding and support degrade as you grow, trading a loved experience for faster acquisition and higher churn. Mistake: celebrating new customers while ignoring the ones quietly leaving. Exit: (a) What turns founder-led selling into something that scales? (b) Why must customer experience scale alongside acquisition? Answers: a documented, repeatable sales engine with defined stages that a new rep can follow; because growth that wins customers while eroding their experience just increases churn and drains the economics.

lessons.title: Growth strategies: expansion, new segments, and new markets
lessons.grammar_note: Order growth bets by risk: selling more to current customers is the safest, and a new product in a brand-new market is the riskiest - pursue the safe bets first.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the main strategies a scale-up uses to keep growing and rank them by risk, so you pursue the safest sources of growth first. Warm-up: is it easier to sell more to a customer who already trusts you, or to win a stranger in a market you have never served?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Once a model works, a scale-up grows along a few well-worn paths. The safest is expansion within the existing base: selling more to current customers through upgrades, add-ons, and renewals - often called expansion revenue, or land and expand. The next is reaching new segments: taking a product that works for one type of customer and adapting it for an adjacent one, for instance moving from small businesses up to larger ones. Then come new markets, usually new geographies or industries, which bring fresh demand but also new competitors, rules, and buying habits. The boldest path is building new products for new customers, which carries the most risk because little of what you know carries over. A simple way to order these is by how much is new: the more new things a bet introduces - new product and new market at once - the greater the risk. Disciplined scale-ups harvest the safe, high-return growth near their core before reaching for distant bets, and they resist chasing many directions at once, which spreads focus thin and stalls all of them. Growth is a portfolio: mostly near-core, with a few measured stretches.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Expansion example: a software company whose customers start on a basic plan and later add seats, modules, and premium support can grow revenue sharply without winning a single new logo - its net revenue from existing customers rises over 100 percent a year. New-segment example: a tool built for freelancers is repackaged, with heavier security and admin controls, for large enterprises - same core product, new buyer. New-market example: a retailer that dominates its home country enters a neighboring one, discovering different regulations, payment habits, and rivals that force real adaptation. New-product example: a payments company launches a lending product to its existing merchants - new product, but a familiar customer, which keeps the risk moderate. The riskiest bet of all is a new product for a market you have never served, because neither the product nor the customer is known. A practical sequence: maximize expansion first, then move to adjacent segments, then new markets, and treat brand-new products as a small, deliberate part of the portfolio rather than the main plan.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each, then check yourself. 1) Which growth path is usually the safest? 2) What is expansion revenue? 3) Give an example of moving into a new segment. 4) Why are new geographic markets riskier than selling more to current customers? 5) Which combination is the riskiest growth bet? 6) Why should a scale-up avoid chasing many directions at once? Answers: 1) Selling more to existing customers. 2) Revenue growth from current customers through upgrades, add-ons, and renewals. 3) Adapting a product built for small businesses to serve large enterprises. 4) Because they bring new competitors, rules, and buying habits you do not yet understand. 5) A new product sold into a market you have never served. 6) Because it spreads focus and resources too thin, stalling every effort.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: chasing shiny new markets while leaving easy expansion revenue sitting untouched in the existing base. Mistake: entering a new country or industry without adapting to its rules, competitors, and buying habits. Mistake: launching a new product for a new customer as a first move rather than a measured stretch. Mistake: pursuing too many growth directions at once, so none gets the focus to work. Exit: (a) Rank these by risk: new segment, expansion within the base, new product in a new market. (b) Why pursue near-core growth first? Answers: expansion within the base is safest, then a new segment, then a new product in a new market is riskiest; near-core growth reuses what you already know, giving higher return for lower risk.

items.example: With a repeatable sales engine in place, the startup had become a scale-up.

lessons.title: Raising growth capital and leading through the transition
lessons.grammar_note: Raise growth capital to accelerate a model that already works, never to discover one; a growth round buys speed, not product-market fit.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why and how a scale-up raises growth capital, and describe how a founder's role changes as the company grows. Warm-up: if early funding is raised to find the model, what is growth-stage funding raised to do instead?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Growth capital is money raised to accelerate a model that already works. Where a seed round funds the search for product-market fit, a growth round - a Series B or later, and sometimes venture debt or revenue-based financing - pours fuel on a proven engine so it can capture a market faster than competitors. Investors at this stage fund metrics, not just vision: they want to see predictable revenue growth, healthy retention, an acquisition cost that pays back, and a clear use for the money. Every round trades ownership for cash, so founders weigh dilution against the speed the capital buys. Raising more than you can deploy well is its own trap, inviting the premature scaling that sinks companies. Alongside the money, the company itself changes, and so must its leaders. The founder's job shifts from doing the work to building the organization that does the work - hiring executives, setting direction, and letting go of decisions they once owned. Some founders grow into chief executives of a large company; others bring in experienced leaders for roles they cannot fill. Scaling is as much a personal transition as a financial one.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Funding example: a company with 3 percent monthly churn, 150 percent net revenue retention, and a sales engine that pays back acquisition cost in under a year raises a Series B to triple its sales team and enter two new markets - fuel on a working fire. Contrast a company that raises the same round with 8 percent churn: the money accelerates losses. Dilution example: selling 20 percent of the company for capital that doubles growth may be worth it; selling 20 percent for cash you cannot deploy is not. Leadership example: a founder who personally approved every hire at 20 people must, at 200, hire a head of sales and a head of operations and trust them, meeting a small leadership team rather than everyone. Transition example: some founders deliberately step into a chairman role and recruit an experienced chief executive, judging that the company needs skills they do not yet have. The through-line: capital and leadership both exist to scale a proven model, and both do harm when they outrun it or cling to old habits.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each, then check yourself. 1) What is growth capital raised to do? 2) Name two metrics growth investors want to see. 3) What does a founder trade away when raising a round? 4) Why is raising more than you can deploy a trap? 5) How does the founder's role change as the company scales? 6) Give one example of a leadership transition at scale. Answers: 1) Accelerate a model that already works, not find one. 2) Any two of: predictable revenue growth, strong retention, recoverable acquisition cost, a clear use of funds. 3) Ownership, through dilution. 4) Because idle or carelessly spent capital invites premature scaling. 5) From doing the work to building and leading the organization that does it. 6) Hiring experienced executives, or stepping aside for a professional chief executive while taking a chairman role.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: raising a growth round before the model is proven, so the capital funds premature scaling. Mistake: optimizing for the biggest headline round rather than the right amount you can deploy well. Mistake: a founder clinging to every decision as the company grows, becoming the bottleneck they warn others about. Mistake: hiring senior leaders and then refusing to give them real authority. Exit: (a) What should be true before raising growth capital? (b) How must a founder's role change to let a company keep scaling? Answers: the model should already work, with metrics like retention and recoverable acquisition cost; the founder must move from doing the work to building the organization and leaders that do it, and actually delegate authority.
